detail: supported
Memory complexity reduces the total interval tree size to approximately 1/8th of a regular interval tree [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and the main text (Section 4.2) that by grouping eight adjacent cells into a single pointer, 'the total size for the entire interval tree would be about 1/8th of the size of a regular interval tree' and 'the total size of the interval tree is about 1/8th of a regular interval tree.' The claim accurately reflects this specific finding regarding memory complexity reduction.
supported
The Interval Tree with Cell Grouping is a memory-optimized variant of the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Interval Tree with Cell Grouping is a memory-optimized variant of the Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction. The evidence explicitly describes this variant in Section 4.2, noting that it reduces memory overhead by having pointers represent groups of eight adjacent cells, resulting in a total size of about 1/8th of a regular interval tree. The context of the document (Section 5 and Section 4.4) confirms its application in isosurface visualization/extraction.
supported
1. **Construction:** Partition the volume into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the volume is partitioned into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 4.2: 'The first approach we have set is to have a pointer to represent a group of eight adjacent cells... Notice that the groups of eight cells are disjoint.' It further explains that 'it is as if we group a set of eight neighbour cells into a new bigger cell' and that the tree stores these new big cells. Therefore, the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
The tree structure mirrors the Standard Interval Tree but uses grouped pointers [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the tree structure mirrors the Standard Interval Tree but uses grouped pointers. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 4.2: 'Figure 3 illustrates a node in this new tree: it is basically the same as the nodes in a normal interval tree... But each pointer now references a set of eight adjacent cells'. This directly supports the claim that the structure mirrors the standard tree while utilizing grouped pointers.
supported
Stop iterating a list as soon as a group is found that does not intersect the query value $q$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that one should stop iterating a list as soon as a group is found that does not intersect the query value q. Source [S1], specifically in Section 4.2 under 'Interval Trees with Cell Grouping', explicitly states: 'The implementation of the query process is simple, because, while we are visiting one of the lists, we can stop iterating as soon as we find a group of eight cells that does not intersect the query value q.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
Within each group, the cell with the lowest coordinates $(x, y, z)$ serves as the representative [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that within each group, the cell with the lowest coordinates (x, y, z) serves as the representative. Source [S1] explicitly states in the notes and the passage: 'inside the group of eight cells, the one with the lowest coordinates is taken as the representative of the set.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
The volume is partitioned into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 4.2 that 'the groups of eight cells are disjoint' and that 'each pointer now references a set of eight adjacent cells'. This directly supports the claim that the volume is partitioned into disjoint groups of eight adjacent cells.
supported
This reduction comes at the cost of increased query time, as intersecting groups require checking all eight constituent cells individually [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the reduction in memory (achieved by grouping cells) comes at the cost of increased query time because intersecting groups require checking all eight constituent cells individually. Source [S1] explicitly supports this in Section 4.2: it states that 'care must be taken since relevant changes in the query procedure may increase the query time' and explains that 'for each of these bigger cells, we still have to check each of the eight composing cells.' It further quantifies this by stating the query complexity becomes O(log(n) + 8*k) in the worst case, and Section 4.4 confirms that 'the tree with only cells' grouping presents the slowest times' compared to the normal interval tree.
supported
The worst-case query complexity degrades to $O(\log(n) + 8k)$ when the isosurface intersects exactly one cell from each group of eight [S1, unofficial].

The source text explicitly states in Section 4.2 that for the interval tree with cell grouping, 'the worst case scenario occurs when an isosurface intersects 1/8 of all the cells in the volume in such a way that it only intersects one cell from each group of eight cells.' It further explains that in this scenario, the term k increases by a factor of eight because all eight sub-cells must be verified, yielding a complexity of O(log(n) + 8*k).
supported
The group's bounding box is defined by the global minimum value $v_{min}$ and global maximum value $v_{max}$ across all eight constituent cells [S1, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'when the minimum and maximum of a cell are obtained, they are actually the global minimum and maximum of the eight cells as a group.' This confirms that the bounding box (defined by min and max values) for a group of eight cells is determined by the global minimum and maximum values across all eight constituent cells.
supported
Query time complexity is $O(\log(n) + 8k)$, where $k$ is the number of active cells in the original un-grouped tree [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and the passage under section 4.2 that the query complexity for the interval tree with cell grouping is O(log(n) + 8*k), where k is the number of active cells in the original tree. The text explains that the factor of 8 arises because, in the worst case, the algorithm must check all eight composing cells within each intersecting group.
supported

The Interval Tree with Cell Grouping was introduced to address the prohibitive memory requirements of standard interval trees for isosurface extraction, which can require up to nine times the size of the volume data [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the total space usage of a standard interval tree (including volume loading) is 'nine times the size of the volume' and that this requirement 'can be prohibitive'. It then introduces the 'Interval Tree with Cell Grouping' specifically as a way to 'decrease the memory overhead', noting that this variant reduces the tree size to about 1/8th of a regular interval tree. Thus, the claim that the variant was introduced to address the prohibitive memory requirements of standard trees (which can be up to nine times the volume size) is fully supported by the text.
supported
For each group, it stores an order vector of eight numbers (1–8) indicating the permutation of cells within the group [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and the passage under section 4.3 that 'for each group of eight cells, we use a vector of eight numbers indicating its order' and that 'each number is between one and eight'. This directly supports the claim that the system stores an order vector of eight numbers (1–8) indicating the permutation of cells within the group.
supported
For each group, compute the global minimum value $v_{min}$ and global maximum value $v_{max}$ across all eight cells [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that for each group, the global minimum value ($v_{min}$) and global maximum value ($v_{max}$) are computed across all eight cells. The source text explicitly confirms this in Section 4.2: 'requiring only that, when the minimum and maximum of a cell are obtained, they are actually the global minimum and maximum of the eight cells as a group.' Additionally, Section 4.3 mentions storing pointers sorted by 'the minimum value of the cell group' and 'the maximum value', implying these aggregate values are computed for the group.
supported
**Inputs:** A 3D scalar volume grid and an isovalue $q$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the inputs are a 3D scalar volume grid and an isovalue q. The provided text describes an algorithm for 'Isosurface Visualization' using interval trees. Section 4.2 explicitly mentions querying for a 'query value q' (isovalue) and checking cells within a volume (implied by the context of 3D grids, adjacent cells, and volume sizes). Section 4.4 confirms tests were run on 'volumes' and queried for 'isosurface values'. Therefore, the evidence supports that the system takes a 3D volume and an isovalue as inputs to perform the described operations.
